title: Umbilical cord prolapse
blurb: Recognise cord prolapse, handle the cord minimally, relieve compression by elevating the presenting part or filling the bladder, position the woman safely and arrange the right category of birth (RCOG GTG 50).
question: At home at 39 weeks, Maya's waters break and her community midwife sees a loop of cord at the vulva. The fetal heart rate is 90 bpm. What should the midwife do while waiting for the ambulance, and how should Maya travel?

teach.body: Formally (RCOG GTG 50): umbilical cord prolapse is the descent of the cord through the cervix alongside the presenting part (occult) or past it (overt), in the presence of ruptured membranes. In plain English: once the waters have gone, the cord slips down beside or in front of the baby, where the baby's head or bottom can squash it, and cord outside the warm vagina can go into spasm. Either way the baby's oxygen supply is cut, so every minute counts.

rows.label: How found
values: Seen or felt at VE or vulva

teach.caption: Incidence 0.1-0.6% of births, higher at about 1% with breech presentation (GTG 50).

steps.label: Call for help
steps.sub: obstetric, anaesthetic, neonatal; 999 if at home

steps.sub: do not try to push it back

steps.label: Relieve compression
steps.sub: elevate presenting part manually or fill the bladder

steps.label: Position
steps.sub: knee-chest, or left lateral head-down with pillow under left hip

teach.caption: If FHR abnormalities persist while preparing for caesarean, tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously) can be considered.

children.label: Assisted vaginal birth

children.edge: Birth not imminent, FHR suspicious or pathological
children.label: Category 1 caesarean
children.sub: aim for birth within 30 minutes or less

values: Elevate presenting part or fill bladder

items.label: terbutaline SC, if tocolysis is used

items: Avoid artificial rupture of membranes when the presenting part is high or mobile, where possible.
For an unstable, transverse or oblique lie, discuss elective admission to hospital after 37+0 weeks.
If membranes rupture with a high or non-cephalic presenting part, think of cord prolapse and check the fetal heart.

teach.body: The midwife calls 999, saying 'cord prolapse', and asks the second midwife or partner to help. She handles the cord as little as possible and does not try to replace it. She asks Maya to go into the knee-chest position, face down, and elevates the presenting part with her fingers or fills Maya's bladder through a Foley catheter. In the ambulance, Maya lies in the exaggerated Sims position, and they go to the nearest consultant-led unit with a pre-alert.

teach.text: Two traps. Do not push the cord back up: manual replacement above the presenting part is not recommended, and handling causes vasospasm. And knee-chest is right at home but unsafe in a moving ambulance, where the exaggerated Sims position is used instead.

items: Cord prolapse = cord past (overt) or alongside (occult) the presenting part with ruptured membranes.
Call for help; minimal handling; do not try to replace the cord.
Elevate the presenting part or fill the bladder; knee-chest or left lateral head-down.
Category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes if FHR suspicious or pathological; assisted vaginal birth if fully dilated and quick.
Community: knee-chest at home, exaggerated Sims in the ambulance, nearest consultant-led unit.

summary: You can now recognise overt and occult cord prolapse, relieve cord compression with minimal handling, positioning and bladder filling, and choose the right category of birth. You can also manage a cord prolapse at home and during transfer.

A.q: A loop of cord is lying outside the vagina after spontaneous rupture of membranes. How should the midwife handle it?
options: Push it gently back above the presenting part
Minimal handling, leaving it where it is
Pull gently to straighten the loop
Clamp and cut it to stop bleeding
A.why: GTG 50: handle loops of cord outside the vagina as little as possible to prevent vasospasm; manual replacement above the presenting part is not recommended.

whyNot.0: Manual replacement of the cord is not recommended.
whyNot.2: Pulling on the cord causes spasm and may worsen compression.
whyNot.3: Cutting the cord would end the baby's oxygen supply.

A.q: On the labour ward, cord prolapse is confirmed and a caesarean is being prepared. Which maternal position helps relieve cord compression?
options: Semi-recumbent and sitting upright in bed
Supine with legs in stirrups
Standing and leaning forwards
Knee-chest or left lateral, head down
A.why: GTG 50: the knee-chest or left lateral position (head down, pillow under the left hip) helps prevent compression of the cord.

whyNot.0: Sitting upright lets the presenting part press down on the cord.
whyNot.1: Supine with legs raised does not reduce compression.
whyNot.2: Standing increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.

A.q: What is an occult cord prolapse?
options: Cord past the presenting part, seen at the vulva
Cord beside the presenting part, after ROM
Cord below the presenting part, membranes intact
Cord around the baby's neck at the birth
A.why: GTG 50: occult prolapse is descent of the cord alongside the presenting part, with ruptured membranes.

whyNot.0: Cord past the presenting part is overt prolapse.
whyNot.2: Cord prolapse needs ruptured membranes; with intact membranes this is not a prolapse.
whyNot.3: A nuchal cord is not a cord prolapse.

B.q: Cord prolapse is diagnosed at 7 cm. The presenting part is elevated but the CTG is pathological. What mode of birth does GTG 50 recommend?
options: Category 1, aiming for birth within 60 minutes
Category 2, as the cord is now protected
Category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes
Category 3, once she has fasted
B.why: GTG 50: caesarean when vaginal birth is not imminent; category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes or less, if the FHR pattern is suspicious or pathological.

whyNot.0: The category 1 target is 30 minutes or less, not 60.
whyNot.1: Category 2 is considered only when the FHR is normal; here it is pathological.
whyNot.3: Delaying for fasting is unsafe with a pathological CTG.

B.q: A woman with cord prolapse is being transferred by ambulance. Which position does GTG 50 recommend for the journey?
options: Knee-chest, face down
Exaggerated Sims position
Supine with a left tilt
Sitting upright and strapped in
B.why: GTG 50: during ambulance transfer the exaggerated Sims position is used, because knee-chest is potentially unsafe in a moving vehicle.

whyNot.0: Knee-chest is advised at home while waiting, but is unsafe in a moving vehicle.
whyNot.2: Supine does not relieve pressure on the cord.
whyNot.3: Sitting upright increases compression of the cord.

B.q: Why does GTG 50 say community midwives should carry a Foley catheter?
options: To fill the bladder, raising the presenting part
To drain her bladder before the ambulance arrives
To guide the cord back up into the uterus
To measure urine output during the transfer
B.why: GTG 50: filling the urinary bladder elevates the presenting part and relieves cord compression; community midwives should carry a Foley catheter for this.

whyNot.1: The aim is to fill, not empty, the bladder.
whyNot.2: The cord should not be replaced.
whyNot.3: Urine output is not the purpose here.

C.q: At home at 39 weeks, Maya's waters break and the midwife sees a loop of cord at the vulva. The fetal heart rate is 90 bpm and Maya is 4 cm dilated. What should the midwife do?
options: Call 999, knee-chest, elevate the presenting part
Replace the cord and drive her to hospital
Encourage pushing for a quick home birth
Await the ambulance sitting semi-recumbent on the sofa
C.why: GTG 50: call for emergency transfer, use the knee-chest face-down position at home, elevate the presenting part (or fill the bladder) and handle the cord minimally.

whyNot.1: The cord must not be replaced, and a car is not a safe transfer.
whyNot.2: At 4 cm, birth is not imminent; pushing will not achieve a quick birth.
whyNot.3: Sitting increases compression of the cord.

C.q: Cord prolapse is diagnosed at full dilatation with the head low. The senior obstetrician judges that birth can be achieved quickly and safely. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Category 2 caesarean section
Assisted vaginal birth now
Tocolysis and await descent
Replace the cord and wait
C.why: GTG 50: assisted vaginal birth can be used at full dilatation when birth can be accomplished quickly and safely.

whyNot.0: A caesarean would take longer than a quick, safe vaginal birth here.
whyNot.2: Waiting prolongs cord compression when birth can be achieved now.
whyNot.3: The cord should not be replaced.

C.q: Lena, 40 weeks, has a high, mobile head after an unstable lie earlier in the third trimester. A colleague suggests artificial rupture of membranes to 'get things going'. Which practice does GTG 50 support?
options: Routine ARM for all women at 4 cm
Perform ARM early in labour to help settle the lie
Avoid ARM if the presenting part is high or mobile
Walk about straight after ARM with a high head
C.why: GTG 50: avoid artificial rupture of membranes when the presenting part is high or mobile, where possible, to reduce the risk of cord prolapse.

whyNot.0: Routine ARM is not advised, especially with a high head.
whyNot.1: ARM with a high or mobile presenting part increases cord prolapse risk.
whyNot.3: This does not address the risk of ARM with a high presenting part.

reteach.title: Lift the baby off the cord
reteach.question: The cord is trapped between the baby and the pelvis. What three ways can you take the pressure off it?

blocks.body: Gravity: knee-chest or head-down left lateral lets the baby fall back away from the pelvis. Fingers: a gloved hand in the vagina pushes the presenting part up off the cord. Fluid: filling the bladder lifts the presenting part from below. Meanwhile, leave the cord alone (handling causes spasm), call for help and get the baby born: category 1 caesarean within 30 minutes if the heart rate is abnormal.

blocks.text: Home: knee-chest. Ambulance: exaggerated Sims. Do not push the cord back: replacement is not recommended.

explain.body: Cord prolapse complicates 0.1-0.6% of births, rising to about 1% with breech presentation (GTG 50).

test.q: How common is cord prolapse when the baby is breech, according to GTG 50?
options: About 1%
About 0.01%
About 10 in every 100
About 1 in every 4
test.why: GTG 50: 'In the case of breech presentation, the incidence is higher at 1%', compared with 0.1-0.6% overall.

whyNot.1: 0.01% is far lower than the overall incidence.

explain.body: Handle loops of cord outside the vagina as little as possible to prevent vasospasm. Do not try to replace the cord above the presenting part (GTG 50).

test.q: Why should cord outside the vagina be handled as little as possible?
options: To keep the cord sterile for clamping
To avoid causing the woman pain
To prevent vasospasm of the cord
To let the cord dry naturally
test.why: GTG 50: minimal handling prevents vasospasm, which would further reduce blood flow to the baby.

whyNot.0: Sterility is not the reason, and the cord is not clamped.
whyNot.1: The cord has no nerves; the concern is the baby's blood flow.
whyNot.3: The cord should not be left to dry; the issue is spasm.

explain.body: If FHR abnormalities persist despite elevating the presenting part, tocolysis can be considered while preparing for caesarean: GTG 50 suggests terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously.

test.q: Which tocolytic does GTG 50 suggest if FHR abnormalities persist while preparing for caesarean?
options: Oxytocin 10 units by IM injection
Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV
Ergometrine 500 micrograms by IM injection
Terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously
test.why: GTG 50 suggests terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously as tocolysis while preparing for caesarean.

whyNot.0: Oxytocin stimulates contractions, the opposite of tocolysis.
whyNot.1: Magnesium sulfate is used for eclampsia and neuroprotection, not this tocolysis.

explain.body: If the FHR pattern is normal and compression is relieved, a category 2 caesarean can be considered; continue to elevate the presenting part and monitor (GTG 50).

test.q: Cord prolapse is confirmed in the first stage. The presenting part is elevated and the FHR remains normal. What does GTG 50 say?
options: Category 2 caesarean can be considered
Expectant management until full dilatation
Category 3 caesarean the next day
Oxytocin to speed up the labour
test.why: GTG 50: category 2 caesarean can be considered when the FHR is normal, with continued measures to relieve compression.

whyNot.1: Expectant management is not appropriate for cord prolapse.
whyNot.2: A next-day caesarean leaves the cord at risk for far too long.
whyNot.3: Speeding labour with oxytocin increases compression.
